title: The amoraim
hookLine: the sages of the Gemara, who discussed the Mishnah for three centuries

cards: A sage is bathing in the Jordan River. A rough stranger sees him from the bank and, in one leap, jumps into the water after him. The sage is Rabbi Yochanan.

The stranger is a man the Talmud calls Resh Lakish, and the story says he had been living as a robber. Rabbi Yochanan says: your strength should be for Torah. Resh Lakish answers: your beauty should be for women.
They strike a deal: if he'll turn to study, Rabbi Yochanan will give him his sister in marriage. He does. And the robber becomes a sage whose words fill the Talmud.

teach.b: Amora. In the plural, amoraim. The tannaim gave the Mishnah its words.

The amoraim are the sages who came after, in the land of Israel and in Babylonia, and spent generations discussing those words line by line. Their discussion is the Gemara. Mishnah plus Gemara: the Talmud.
The word is Aramaic, and Jastrow's dictionary ties it to the verb to say: a speaker, an expounder.
A few pairs to know: Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish in the land of Israel, and later Abaye and Rava. They're remembered in pairs. Explaining was done with someone.
Back to the riverbank, in tractate Bava Metzia. Years later, after a bitter quarrel, Resh Lakish dies, and Rabbi Yochanan is crushed. The sages send him a brilliant student, Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat.

teach.h: AMORA: ONE WHO SAYS, WHO EXPOUNDS.
teach.b: Whatever Rabbi Yochanan says, Rabbi Elazar answers: there's a teaching that supports you.

teach.h: RAV AND SHMUEL; ABAYE AND RAVA.
teach.b: Rabbi Yochanan can't bear it. In paraphrase: are you like the son of Lakish?

teach.h: TWENTY-FOUR OBJECTIONS, AND IT CAME CLEAR.
teach.b: When I said something, he raised twenty-four objections, I gave twenty-four answers, and the matter came clear on its own. You only tell me I'm right.
I know I'm right. The story ends in grief, with Rabbi Yochanan crying out for his friend. For the amoraim, explaining wasn't agreeing.
It was pushing back, hard, until the teaching came clear.

how: Talmud study is traditionally done in pairs, a chavruta, where two learners read aloud, question each other and argue their way to the meaning of a passage.

o: a poet who wrote the prayers for festivals
a sage of the Gemara who explained the Mishnah
a judge who settled disputes in the market

p: kept saying, a teaching supports you

s: the tannaim gave the Mishnah its words. the amoraim discussed it, line by line, in the Gemara.
Rabbi Yochanan missed a partner who argued with him
he said Resh Lakish raised twenty-four objections, and through the answers the matter became clear.
the best study partner is one who always agrees
Rabbi Yochanan couldn't bear a partner who only told him he was right.

games.q: you're Rabbi Yochanan. your partner in study has died. the sages send you a brilliant student who supports every word you say. what do you do?
o: welcome the support and go on teaching.
tell him you need objections, not agreement.
games.why: he asks, are you like the son of Lakish? he raised twenty-four objections, and the answers made the matter clear. the story ends in his grief.

practice: Say the name Resh Lakish quietly a few times, the man who leapt into the river, until it stays. Then bring to mind someone who pushes back on you in a way that leaves you clearer instead of smaller, and hold their face for a while.
If you pray, you can give thanks for them; if not, just notice what they've given you.

wordCard.voice: Amora. One of the sages of the Gemara, who discussed the Mishnah line by line, tied in the dictionary to the verb to say. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic: a sage of the Gemara; plural amoraim, אָמוֹרָאִים.

carryVoice: Your line: the explainers. A friend who pushes back can leave you clearer, not smaller. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Marcus Jastrow, A Dictionary of the Targumim, the Talmud Babli and Yerushalmi, and the Midrashic Literature (1903), s.v. amora
